question:
A 87-year-old female patient presents for follow-up of hypertension and reports noticing a swelling in
the anterior triangle of her neck over the past 12 to 18 months. She denies symptoms such as weight
changes, palpitations, muscle weakness, skin or voice changes, or neck pain. She has no history of
radiation exposure or family history of thyroid cancer. On examination, her blood pressure is 137/93
mm Hg, heart rate is 92 beats per minute, and temperature is 36.5°C. A 2- to 3-cm swelling is observed
at the base of the neck, just to the right of the trachea, which moves upward with swallowing. The
swelling is non-tender, not tethered to the skin, and there is no lymphadenopathy. The palms are
slightly diaphoretic, but no other signs of thyroid dysfunction are noted. Laboratory results are as
follows: | | Patient value | Reference range | | --- | --- | --- | | Thyroid-stimulating hormone (μU/mL) | 0.03
| 0.5–4.7 | | Calcium (mg/dL) | 9.4 | 9.0–10.5 | | Phosphorus (mg/dL) | 3.6 | 3.0–4.5 | | Albumin (g/dL) |
3.8 | 3.5–5.5 | The complete blood count is within normal limits. What is the most appropriate next step
in evaluating this patient? Answer Choices: (A) Surgical excision of the nodule for histopathology (B)
PET scan to evaluate for malignancy (C) Thyroid ultrasound and fine-needle aspiration of the nodule
(D) Repeat TSH measurement in 6 weeks (E) Empirical treatment with antithyroid medication (F)
Measurement of thyroid-stimulating immunoglobulin (G) CT scan of the neck and chest (H)
Radionuclide scanning with iodine-123 (I) Measurement of free T4 and total T3 levels (J) Fine-needle
aspiration without imaging guidance
 A. Thyroid ultrasound and fine-needle aspiration of the nodule
